title: Insurance Funds: Investment and Asset-Liability Management

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the investment mandate of a life insurance company — why life insurers invest premiums, what objectives govern the investment function, and how the investment strategy connects to the insurer’s pricing, reserving, and solvency obligations.

Describe the statutory separation of life and non-life insurance funds, explain the rationale for separate fund management, and identify the regulatory consequences of fund commingling under NIIRA 2025.

Identify the principal classes of admissible assets for Nigerian life insurance funds and describe the investment restrictions and concentration limits imposed by NAICOM and by the NIIRA 2025 framework.

Explain the concept of asset-liability matching (ALM) and describe how duration matching and cash flow matching are applied in a Nigerian life insurance context to manage interest rate risk and liquidity risk.

Describe the principal investment classes used by Nigerian life insurers — government securities, equities, real estate, and money market instruments — and assess the risk-return profile and ALM implications of each.

Apply the principles of modern portfolio theory to the construction of a life insurance investment portfolio, explaining how diversification, correlation, the efficient frontier, and the risk-return trade-off are balanced in the insurance investment context.

Describe the Nigerian capital market infrastructure — the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the FMDQ Exchange (fixed income), and the Central Securities Clearing System (CSCS) — and explain the regulatory interactions between insurance investment and capital market regulation.

Explain the regulatory framework for foreign currency assets and cross-border holdings in Nigerian life insurance portfolios, including CBN restrictions and the NAICOM admissible asset rules for foreign currency instruments.

Analyse the impact of Nigeria’s high and volatile interest rate environment on the solvency position of Nigerian life insurers, and describe the specific mechanisms through which interest rate movements affect the valuation of liabilities and assets.

Describe NIIRA 2025’s investment obligations for life insurers, including the admissible asset requirements, NAICOM’s investment reporting obligations, the ALCO governance requirement, and NAICOM’s supervisory powers over the investment function.

blocks.text: 23.1 Introduction: The Investment Function in Life Insurance

blocks.h: A life insurance company is simultaneously an insurance business and an investment business. When a policyholder pays a premium, most of that money does not immediately flow back out as claims — it is held for months, years, or decades until the policy matures, the insured dies, or the policyholder surrenders. During this holding period, the insurer invests the premium, and the investment return generated is a fundamental component of the insurer’s commercial model.

For a participating endowment policy with a 20-year term, the investment return earned on the accumulated reserve over the full 20 years contributes a significant portion of the maturity benefit. For an annuity product, the insurer must earn investment returns sufficient to fund the guaranteed income payments for the full lifetime of the annuitant, which may extend for 20–30 years or more beyond the annuity commencement date. For a whole life policy, the insurer invests premiums for the entire active duration of the policy, which may be 40–50 years.

The investment function is therefore not peripheral to a life insurer’s business — it is central. The return assumption embedded in product pricing, the interest rate used to discount policy reserves in the actuarial valuation, and the yield on the investment portfolio are three expressions of the same underlying reality: the life insurer’s financial health depends critically on earning adequate, reliable, and sustainable investment returns over very long time horizons.

In the Nigerian context, the investment function operates under conditions that are unusually challenging: high nominal interest rates (which generate attractive short-term yields but create asset-liability duration mismatch risk when rates inevitably fall); a domestic bond market that lacks the depth and duration required for long-term liability matching; an equity market that is volatile and relatively illiquid for large institutional holdings; and a regulatory framework that has historically lagged the sophistication of the investment management challenge. NIIRA 2025 represents a significant step toward a more rigorous investment governance regime, introducing new admissible asset criteria, NAICOM investment reporting requirements, and ALCO governance obligations.

blocks.text: 23.2 The Investment Mandate of a Life Insurer

blocks.h: The investment mandate of a life insurance company is the set of objectives, constraints, and guidelines that govern how the investment portfolio is managed. Unlike a hedge fund (whose mandate may be to maximise absolute return regardless of volatility) or a pension fund (whose mandate is to maximise the probability of meeting future pension payments), the life insurer’s investment mandate must balance several objectives simultaneously:

rows: Capital preservation

The insurer must not lose the policyholder’s premium. Capital preservation is the primary obligation: the investment portfolio must not be managed in a way that puts the principal at material risk. This means that speculative, highly leveraged, or illiquid investment strategies are inconsistent with the insurance investment mandate.
Liability matching

The investment portfolio must be structured to generate cash flows that align with the timing and amount of the insurer’s expected policy liability outflows. A 20-year endowment creates a liability that matures in 20 years; the investment portfolio should include assets with 20-year maturities to match this liability.
Adequate return on assets

The investment portfolio must earn a return at least equal to the investment return assumption embedded in the pricing of the insurer’s products. If the pricing assumes a 12% p.a. investment return and the portfolio only earns 9%, the pricing assumption is violated and the product will be unprofitable.
Liquidity management

The insurer must have sufficient liquid assets to meet unexpected cash demands: a surge in claims (pandemic or catastrophe scenario), a wave of policy surrenders, or a regulatory capital requirement increase. Investing exclusively in long-duration illiquid assets (property, private placements) creates liquidity risk that is inconsistent with the insurance mandate.
Regulatory compliance

The investment portfolio must comply with NAICOM’s admissible asset requirements, concentration limits, and fund separation rules at all times. Non-compliant investments do not count toward the insurer’s regulatory capital base.
Risk management

The investment portfolio must be managed within the risk limits set by the Board in the investment policy statement, including limits on market risk, credit risk, liquidity risk, and currency risk. The investment function is a key component of the ERM framework (Chapter 15).

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 requires every life insurer to establish an Asset-Liability Management Committee (ALCO) as the governance body responsible for overseeing the investment function and ensuring that the investment strategy remains consistent with the liability profile. The ALCO is typically chaired by the CFO or CIO and includes the Statutory Actuary, the Chief Risk Officer, the Head of Investment, and senior representatives from the product and underwriting functions.

The ALCO’s mandate includes: approving the investment policy statement; setting and monitoring asset-liability duration gap limits; reviewing the investment portfolio’s compliance with NAICOM admissible asset requirements quarterly; approving any deviation from the investment policy limits; and reporting investment performance and ALM metrics to the Board on a quarterly basis. The ALCO is the organisational interface between the investment function and the risk management framework, ensuring that investment decisions are made with full awareness of their impact on the insurer’s liability obligations.

blocks.text: 23.3 Statutory Separation of Life and Non-Life Funds

blocks.h: Nigerian insurance law — rooted in the Insurance Act 2003 and reinforced by NIIRA 2025 — requires that a composite insurer (one licensed to write both life and non-life insurance) must maintain completely separate, identifiable funds for its life insurance business and its non-life insurance business. The life insurance fund consists of all premiums, investment income, and other receipts attributable to life policies, and it must be used exclusively to meet life policy obligations. It cannot be drawn upon to meet non-life insurance claims, operating expenses of the non-life business, or shareholder dividends beyond the amount actuarially available for distribution.

The separate fund maintained by a life insurer (or the life insurance subsidiary of a composite group) into which all life insurance premiums, investment income attributable to life assets, and other life insurance receipts are paid. The assets of the statutory life insurance fund are held in trust for the benefit of life policyholders and may not be applied to meet non-life obligations or distributed to shareholders without the prior approval of NAICOM and the concurrence of the Statutory Actuary.

The rationale for statutory fund separation is policyholder protection: life insurance policyholders make long-term financial commitments to a company based on the expectation that the premiums they pay are segregated and protected for their benefit. Without fund separation, the life fund’s assets could be raided to meet the obligations of a failing non-life book, leaving life policyholders exposed to a solvency deficit arising from risks they did not knowingly take.
In practice, fund separation requires:

items.h: Separate accounting: The life fund and the non-life fund must be separately accounted for in the insurer’s books, with all income, expense, and asset movements attributed to the correct fund.
Separate investment portfolios: The assets backing the life fund must be physically identified and segregated from the assets backing the non-life fund and the shareholders’ fund.
Separate custody: Ideally (and for large portfolios, practically required), the life fund’s investment assets are held in separate custody accounts, clearly designated as life fund assets.

Actuarial certification: The Statutory Actuary must annually certify that the assets of the life fund are at least equal to the total life insurance liabilities, confirming that the life fund is solvent on a standalone basis.

blocks.title: NIIRA 2025: Consequences of Life and Non-Life Fund Commingling

blocks.h: Fund commingling — the mixing of life insurance fund assets with non-life or shareholders’ fund assets — is a serious regulatory breach under NIIRA 2025:

items.h: Financial penalty of up to ₦50,000,000 for an insurer that fails to maintain the required statutory fund separation.

NAICOM may direct the insurer to restore the fund separation within a defined remediation period. Failure to restore separation within the directed period may result in appointment of a special examiner.

The Statutory Actuary who certifies the insurer’s accounts when fund commingling is present faces personal professional liability under the Insurance Act and may be reported to the actuarial professional body.
Directors of the insurer are personally liable where fund commingling is found to have been deliberate and to have prejudiced policyholder interests.

blocks.h: Admissible assets are the classes of investment that NAICOM recognises as qualifying assets for the purposes of meeting the life fund’s liabilities and the insurer’s regulatory capital requirements under the RBC framework. An investment in a non-admissible asset does not count toward the insurer’s regulatory solvency position: from NAICOM’s perspective, the asset effectively does not exist for solvency purposes.

The admissible asset framework serves two purposes: it protects policyholders by limiting the investment of life fund assets to instruments with defined quality, liquidity, and risk characteristics; and it creates a common, verifiable basis for NAICOM’s supervisory assessment of insurer solvency. An insurer that invests its life fund in non-admissible assets may appear technically solvent on a gross balance sheet basis while being insolvent on the regulatory basis that counts.

blocks.h: Note: Specific limits are determined by NAICOM’s Investment Guidelines, which are periodically updated. Insurers should refer to the most current NAICOM investment guidelines for exact limits. The above reflects approximate market practice under the current framework.

Assets that are not admissible for the life fund include: unlisted private company equity; speculative derivatives (options, futures used for speculation rather than hedging); unsecured personal loans; assets outside Nigeria without CBN and NAICOM approval; cryptocurrencies and digital assets; and any investment that creates a direct conflict of interest with the insurer’s directors or major shareholders (related-party investments require specific NAICOM approval and are subject to strict limitations).

The investment management discipline of structuring the insurer’s investment portfolio so that the cash flows generated by the assets (interest, dividends, and maturing principal) correspond in timing and amount to the cash flows required to meet policy liabilities (claims, maturities, and expenses) as they fall due. Perfect ALM eliminates interest rate risk and liquidity risk from the insurer’s balance sheet; imperfect ALM (a mismatch between asset and liability profiles) creates risks that can materially affect solvency.

ALM is the central discipline of insurance investment management. An insurer that invests 20-year endowment policy reserves in 91-day Treasury bills has a severe duration mismatch: it must reinvest the T-bill proceeds every 91 days, accepting whatever interest rate the market offers at each reinvestment date. If rates fall from 22% to 10% over the course of the 20-year policy, the T-bill investment strategy will generate far less than the return assumed in the pricing — producing losses and policyholder benefit shortfalls. An insurer that matches its 20-year liability with a 20-year FGN bond locks in the investment return for the full liability duration, eliminating this reinvestment risk.

A measure of the interest rate sensitivity of a fixed-income instrument or a portfolio. Specifically, modified duration expresses the approximate percentage change in the price of a bond or portfolio for a 1% change in interest rates. A bond with modified duration of 8 years will fall in price by approximately 8% if interest rates rise by 1%. Duration is the primary ALM metric: by matching the duration of the asset portfolio to the duration of the liability portfolio, the insurer minimises the net impact of interest rate movements on its surplus.
Duration(Assets) ≈ Duration(Liabilities)

When asset duration equals liability duration, a parallel shift in interest rates affects the value of assets and liabilities by approximately the same amount, leaving the surplus (assets minus liabilities) unchanged. When asset duration is shorter than liability duration (a positive duration gap), rising interest rates improve the surplus (asset values fall less than liability values). When asset duration is longer than liability duration (a negative duration gap), rising interest rates destroy surplus.
Duration Gap = Duration(Assets) − Duration(Liabilities). Target: Duration Gap close to zero. NAICOM/ALCO typically sets a tolerance band (e.g., gap between −1 and +1 year).

This is a POSITIVE duration gap problem from the insurer’s perspective: if interest rates FALL (which is the medium-term risk in Nigeria’s high-rate environment), the liabilities will increase in value (as the discount rate falls) by more than the assets, destroying surplus. Cash flow matching is a more precise (and more conservative) ALM approach than duration matching. Rather than managing the aggregate duration of the portfolio, cash flow matching involves constructing the asset portfolio so that the specific cash flows generated by assets on specific future dates are sufficient to meet the specific liability cash flows due on those dates.

For a life insurer with a large annuity book, cash flow matching might involve purchasing a sequence of bonds that mature (or generate coupon payments) in each future year, with the maturity or coupon proceeds exactly equal to the annuity payments due in that year. This approach eliminates both reinvestment risk (no need to reinvest maturing proceeds at uncertain future rates) and liquidity risk (cash is available exactly when needed) but is operationally complex and may not be achievable in the Nigerian bond market where long-dated bonds are limited in availability.

blocks.text: 23.6 Principal Investment Classes for Nigerian Life Insurers
23.6.1 Government Securities: FGN Bonds and Treasury Bills

blocks.h: Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN) bonds are the highest-quality, most liquid domestic fixed-income instrument available to Nigerian life insurers. They are issued by the Debt Management Office (DMO) and traded on the FMDQ Securities Exchange. They carry sovereign credit risk — which, while not zero, is the lowest available in the Nigerian market. Maturities range from 2 to 30 years, providing the duration options necessary for liability matching.

The Nigerian bond market has grown significantly since 2000, and long-dated FGN bonds (15–30 year maturities) are increasingly available. These are the most important instruments for ALM in Nigerian life insurance: they provide long-duration, sovereign-quality assets whose coupon payments and maturities can be aligned with long-term life insurance liabilities. However, the market for very long-dated bonds remains thinner than in mature markets, and large institutional purchases can move prices.

FGN Treasury Bills (T-Bills) are short-term (91–364 day) discount instruments. They are fully liquid, near-zero credit risk, and earn the shortest-maturity segment of the sovereign yield curve. For life insurers, T-bills are appropriate for: the liquidity reserve (the portion of the portfolio held to meet unexpected cash demands); and short-term investment of premium income received while long-term investment decisions are being made. Their limitation is duration: a portfolio dominated by T-bills creates severe reinvestment risk for long-term liabilities.

Listed Nigerian equities — traded on the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) — offer higher expected returns over the long term than fixed-income instruments, reflecting the equity risk premium that compensates investors for bearing the higher volatility and residual claim priority of equities relative to bonds. For long-term life insurance portfolios, a measured allocation to equities is consistent with maximising long-term returns, provided the allocation is within NAICOM’s admissible limits and the portfolio does not create liquidity risk.
The characteristics of the Nigerian equity market that define its suitability for life insurance investment include:

items.h: Market breadth: The NGX lists over 150 companies across banking, consumer goods, oil and gas, industrial goods, and financial services sectors. The market capitalisation is dominated by a small number of large-cap names (MTN Nigeria, Dangote Cement, Airtel Africa, GTCO, Zenith Bank), creating concentration risk for large institutional portfolios.

Liquidity: Daily trading volumes on the NGX are relatively low compared to larger African exchanges. A life insurer with a large equity portfolio may find it difficult to liquidate positions quickly without moving market prices, creating liquidity risk in stress scenarios.

Valuation and dividend income: Nigerian listed equities have historically provided substantial dividend income as well as capital appreciation. Dividend yields on many blue-chip Nigerian companies have been comparable to fixed-income yields, providing income that supports the insurance portfolio’s cash flow needs.

Currency and macroeconomic sensitivity: Nigerian equity market performance is strongly influenced by macroeconomic conditions — oil price movements, currency depreciation, and interest rate policy. A portfolio with a significant equity allocation must be managed with awareness of these macro sensitivities.

blocks.h: Real estate is an important investment class for Nigerian life insurers, offering several characteristics that align well with long-term life insurance liabilities: it is a real (inflation-linked) asset; it generates regular rental income; it has a long economic life that matches long-duration liabilities; and it provides diversification from the financial market correlation of bonds and equities.

Nigerian commercial and residential property has delivered strong returns in Naira terms over the past two decades, driven by urbanisation, population growth, and the expansion of Nigeria’s middle class. However, real estate investment carries material risks for life insurers: illiquidity (large property positions cannot be liquidated quickly without significant discount to market value); valuation uncertainty (professional valuations are required but may not fully reflect market clearing prices); and concentration risk (a large property portfolio in Lagos commercial real estate is exposed to the specific demand conditions of that market).

NAICOM’s admissible asset rules require that real estate investments in the life fund be professionally valued at least annually by a NAICOM-approved valuer, and that the valuation methodology be consistent, documented, and auditable. Properties with disputed ownership, pending litigation, or unusual occupancy structures may not qualify as fully admissible.

Money market instruments — call account deposits, fixed deposits with approved banks, commercial paper, and banker’s acceptances — are the liquidity component of the life insurance investment portfolio. They mature within one year, carry low credit risk where the counterparty is a well-rated bank, and provide instant or very short-notice liquidity.

In Nigeria’s high interest rate environment, money market instruments have historically offered attractive nominal yields relative to their very low credit risk. However, for life insurance ALM purposes, they should represent only the portion of the portfolio needed for operational liquidity and short-term premium receipt investment. An excessive allocation to money market instruments creates the reinvestment risk scenario described in Section 23.5: yield rates that are attractive today may be unavailable on reinvestment, creating a mismatch between the pricing assumption and the actual portfolio yield.

blocks.text: 23.7 Portfolio Theory Applied to Insurance Investment

blocks.h: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), developed by Harry Markowitz in the 1950s, demonstrates that combining assets whose returns are less than perfectly correlated produces a portfolio whose risk (measured by return volatility) is lower than the weighted average risk of its individual components. This is the principle of diversification: spreading investment across multiple asset classes and instruments reduces the impact of any single adverse event on the portfolio’s overall value.
For a Nigerian life insurer, the key correlation relationships that drive diversification benefit are:

items.h: Bonds and equities: In most market environments, bond prices and equity prices move in opposite directions (negative or low positive correlation): when economic conditions deteriorate, equity prices fall but sovereign bond prices rise as investors seek safety. A portfolio combining bonds and equities therefore has lower volatility than either asset class alone.

Fixed income and real estate: Real estate prices are less correlated with bond price movements than equities, providing additional diversification. Both generate income; real estate provides inflation protection that bonds do not.

Naira and foreign currency assets: Where the insurer holds a defined allocation to foreign currency assets (within NAICOM limits), these provide a hedge against Naira depreciation scenarios that would reduce the real value of Naira-denominated assets relative to the insurer’s foreign currency liabilities.

blocks.text: 23.7.2 The Efficient Frontier and the Insurance Investment Constraint

blocks.h: The efficient frontier is the set of investment portfolios that maximise expected return for a given level of risk (or minimise risk for a given expected return). A portfolio on the efficient frontier is fully diversified in the Markowitz sense: no other combination of assets offers a better risk-return trade-off.

For a life insurer, the efficient frontier cannot be the only guide to portfolio construction because the insurer faces constraints that a pure return-maximiser does not: the regulatory admissible asset limits constrain the feasible portfolio space; the ALM obligation requires that the portfolio’s duration profile reflects the liability profile, not merely the return-risk optimum; and the liquidity requirement forces a minimum allocation to liquid instruments that may not be on the unconstrained efficient frontier.

In practice, the insurance investment team constructs a ‘constrained efficient frontier’ that represents the best achievable risk-return combinations within all regulatory and ALM constraints. The ALCO approves the portfolio allocation within this constrained frontier, balancing the competing objectives of maximum return, adequate ALM performance, regulatory compliance, and sufficient liquidity.

blocks.h: Insurance companies that manage their own investment portfolios (rather than delegating to an SEC-registered asset manager) must comply with SEC’s regulations for institutional investors. Key SEC compliance obligations for insurance portfolio managers include:

items.h: Insider trading prohibition: Insurance investment team members who receive material non-public information in the course of their business relationships (e.g., information about a listed company obtained through a corporate insurance client relationship) must not use that information in investment decisions. Insurance companies must maintain information barriers between their business functions and their investment function.

Large shareholder disclosure: An insurance company that acquires more than 5% of the outstanding shares of any single listed company must disclose the holding to the NGX and SEC. Acquisition of 10% or more may trigger additional regulatory requirements.

Investment management registration: Where the insurance company delegates investment management to an external asset manager, that manager must be registered with SEC as an investment adviser or portfolio manager.

blocks.text: 23.9 Foreign Currency Assets and Cross-Border Holdings
23.9.1 The Regulatory Framework for Foreign Currency Investment

blocks.h: Nigerian life insurers face a complex dual-regulatory framework for foreign currency investment: NAICOM’s admissible asset rules set the maximum proportion of the life fund that may be invested in foreign currency instruments; and the CBN’s foreign exchange management regulations govern the mechanics of converting Naira to foreign currency for investment and repatriating foreign currency proceeds.

NAICOM’s admissible asset guidelines permit life insurers to hold a defined percentage of the life fund in foreign currency assets (typically up to 15–20%), subject to: the assets being held with approved custodians in approved jurisdictions; the assets meeting quality standards comparable to Nigerian admissible assets (investment-grade rated, listed on approved exchanges); and the foreign currency holdings being reported to NAICOM in the quarterly investment return.

Foreign currency assets create currency risk in the life insurance portfolio: if the Naira appreciates against the foreign currency in which the assets are denominated, the Naira value of the foreign currency assets declines, reducing the portfolio’s market value. Conversely, if the Naira depreciates (as it did significantly in 2023 and 2024), the Naira value of foreign currency assets rises, generating mark-to-market gains.

The currency risk management challenge for Nigerian life insurers is asymmetric: policies are denominated in Naira, so liabilities are Naira-denominated. Foreign currency assets provide a partial hedge against Naira depreciation (the Naira value of the assets rises with depreciation) and a source of investment income in a foreign currency that may offer lower nominal yields but more stable real returns than Naira instruments. The insurer must decide, within its investment policy, what proportion of the portfolio to hold in foreign currency as a deliberate currency risk and inflation hedge, balanced against the currency risk this creates when the Naira appreciates.

blocks.text: 23.10 The Impact of the Interest Rate Environment on Solvency

blocks.h: Nigeria has historically operated in a high nominal interest rate environment, driven by elevated inflation, currency depreciation expectations, and the CBN’s monetary policy responses. The 12-month Treasury bill rate in Nigeria exceeded 22% in 2024 — a rate that, while attractive in nominal terms for short-duration investment, creates significant actuarial and ALM challenges for life insurers.

The challenge is not the high rate itself — high rates generate attractive current investment income. The challenge is the valuation of long-term liabilities: high current rates used to discount future policy obligations reduce the present value of those obligations, making the insurer appear better capitalised than it would be at lower rates. When rates inevitably normalise (fall), the discount rate used in the liability valuation falls, and the present value of long-term liabilities increases dramatically — potentially revealing a solvency deficit that the high-rate environment had concealed.
A simplified illustration of interest rate sensitivity for a life insurer:

Consider a life insurer with a 20-year endowment portfolio with an aggregate nominal maturity value of ₦100 billion, payable in 20 years. Discounted at 22% p.a.: PV of liabilities ≈ ₦4.3 billion. Discounted at 12% p.a.: PV of liabilities ≈ ₦10.4 billion. Discounted at 8% p.a.: PV of liabilities ≈ ₦21.5 billion.

A fall in the valuation discount rate from 22% to 8% increases the present value of this liability by ₦17.2 billion — a more than five-fold increase. An insurer whose portfolio earns 22% today but whose liabilities are discounted at 22% (matching) has adequate solvency. An insurer whose discount rate falls to 8% but whose T-bill portfolio can only reinvest at 8% faces a liability explosion that may not be covered by the asset portfolio.

For Nigerian life insurers that have historically invested predominantly in short-duration instruments (T-bills and money market deposits), the reinvestment risk is severe: when today’s T-bills mature, the insurer must reinvest at whatever rate is available in the market at that time. If rates have fallen from 22% to 12%, the portfolio’s yield is materially lower than the pricing assumption, and the insurer’s ability to meet its long-term benefit obligations is compromised.

The structural solution to reinvestment risk is to lock in today’s high rates by purchasing long-dated FGN bonds with maturities that match the liability duration. An insurer that purchases a 20-year FGN bond at 18% today locks in that yield for 20 years, regardless of what happens to short-term rates. This is the core ALM discipline: use today’s high-rate environment to extend asset duration toward the liability duration, rather than riding the high short-term rates and accepting the risk of reinvestment at lower rates in the future.

blocks.text: 23.11 NIIRA 2025: Investment Obligations and NAICOM Oversight

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 requires every licensed life insurer to maintain a written Investment Policy Statement (IPS), approved by the Board of Directors and reviewed at least annually. The IPS must include: the insurer’s investment objectives, risk tolerance, and ALM targets; the approved asset classes and concentration limits; the currency risk management approach; the liquidity management requirements; the ALCO governance structure and meeting frequency; and the investment performance benchmarks against which portfolio managers are evaluated.

The IPS is the foundational governance document for the investment function. An investment decision that is inconsistent with the IPS — even if commercially attractive in isolation — is a governance breach that requires Board approval for an IPS amendment or a specific exception. NAICOM may request the IPS as part of its annual supervisory review and may require the insurer to revise provisions that are inconsistent with prudent investment standards.
NIIRA 2025 requires quarterly investment reporting to NAICOM, using the prescribed return format. The quarterly investment return must include:

items.h: A full schedule of investments by asset class, instrument, issuer, and market value, with each investment categorised as admissible or non-admissible.

The calculated coverage ratio: total admissible assets as a percentage of total life insurance liabilities. NAICOM requires the coverage ratio to be maintained above 100% at all times; a ratio below 100% constitutes a regulatory deficiency requiring immediate remediation.
The asset-liability duration gap, calculated using NAICOM’s prescribed methodology.
Any changes in investment policy or significant portfolio restructuring since the last quarterly return.
Investment income received in the quarter, segmented by asset class.
Any investment-related related-party transactions, with disclosure of the nature of the relationship and the basis on which the transaction was assessed as being on arm’s length terms.

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 significantly strengthens NAICOM’s powers in relation to the investment function. These powers include:

items.h: Directed divestment: NAICOM may direct a life insurer to divest a specific investment within a defined period where NAICOM has determined that the investment is non-admissible, creates an unacceptable concentration risk, or is inconsistent with the insurer’s IPS. The insurer may request a review of the direction, but must comply with the direction pending the review outcome.

Investment freeze: NAICOM may freeze the insurer’s investment activities (prevent new investments and restrict asset disposals) where NAICOM has concerns about the solvency of the life fund. An investment freeze is typically accompanied by a special examination of the insurer’s financial position.

Appointed investment manager: Where NAICOM determines that the insurer’s investment management is materially deficient and represents a risk to policyholders, NAICOM may require the appointment of a NAICOM-approved investment manager to manage the life fund until the deficiency is remediated.

Coverage ratio enforcement: Where the coverage ratio falls below 100%, NAICOM has immediate authority to restrict the insurer from paying dividends, making shareholder distributions, or writing new business until the coverage ratio is restored.

blocks.text: 23.12 Advisory: Investment Management Best Practices for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: The investment function in Nigerian life insurance is in transition. The historical model — a simple portfolio of T-bills and money market deposits managed by the finance team with minimal actuarial input and no ALCO governance — is being replaced by a more sophisticated, ALM-driven, institutionally managed approach. This transition is driven by NIIRA 2025’s governance requirements, the growing complexity of the insurance liability profile, and the competitive pressure to earn better risk-adjusted returns.

blocks.title: Advisory: The Investment Function Transformation Agenda for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: PRIORITY 1: ESTABLISH A FUNCTIONING ALCO. The ALCO is not a reporting committee — it is a decision-making body. An ALCO that meets quarterly to review a spreadsheet of investment positions and minutes that no action was required is not managing the investment function; it is observing it. A functioning ALCO: sets the duration target and monitors the duration gap monthly; challenges the investment team on asset allocation decisions; reviews the coverage ratio against both the regulatory minimum and the insurer’s management target; and escalates to the Board when any parameter is breached.

PRIORITY 2: EXTEND DURATION — NOW. The high Nigerian interest rate environment of 2023–2025 is an asset-liability management opportunity that Nigerian life insurers should be exploiting. By purchasing long-dated FGN bonds at today’s yields, insurers can lock in rates that are dramatically above the return assumption embedded in most in-force product pricing. The risk of not acting — continuing to roll short-duration T-bills and accepting tomorrow’s lower reinvestment rate — is far greater than the mark-to-market risk of holding long-dated bonds while rates remain elevated.

PRIORITY 3: INVEST IN INVESTMENT TALENT. The investment function of a life insurer is a specialised financial role. It requires professionals who understand fixed income mathematics, portfolio construction, ALM principles, and the Nigerian capital market. Many Nigerian life insurers manage billions of naira in investment assets with insufficient specialist talent. The cost of hiring a qualified CFA charterholder or investment professional with institutional asset management experience is trivial relative to the value of even modest improvements in portfolio yield or risk management.

PRIORITY 4: BUILD INVESTMENT GOVERNANCE DOCUMENTATION. An Investment Policy Statement that specifies the insurer’s objectives, constraints, and benchmarks is not optional under NIIRA 2025 — it is mandatory. But beyond compliance, a well-crafted IPS disciplines the investment decision-making process: it prevents ad-hoc concentration in a single asset class; it creates accountability for underperformance; and it provides a clear framework for NAICOM’s supervisory engagement with the investment function. Every insurer should have an IPS that is Board-approved, actuary-reviewed, and genuinely used to guide investment decisions.

The set of objectives, constraints, and guidelines that govern how a life insurer’s investment portfolio is managed, including return targets, risk tolerance, ALM requirements, admissible asset classes, and regulatory compliance obligations.

The separate fund maintained by a life insurer into which all life insurance premiums and investment income are paid, held in trust for life policyholders and segregated from non-life and shareholder funds.
The regulatory requirement that composite insurers maintain completely separate, identifiable funds for life and non-life insurance business, preventing cross-subsidisation between fund types.
Investment instruments recognised by NAICOM as qualifying assets for the purpose of meeting life fund liabilities and regulatory capital requirements under the RBC framework.

The investment management discipline of structuring the portfolio so that asset cash flows correspond in timing and amount to policy liability cash flows, managing interest rate risk and liquidity risk.
A measure of a bond or portfolio’s sensitivity to interest rate changes, expressed as the approximate percentage price change for a 1% change in interest rates.

The difference between the duration of the investment portfolio (assets) and the duration of the policy liabilities. A positive gap means assets are shorter in duration than liabilities; a negative gap means assets are longer.
An ALM approach in which the specific cash flows generated by assets on specific dates are structured to exactly match the specific liability cash flows due on those dates.
The governance body responsible for overseeing the investment function and ensuring the investment strategy remains consistent with the liability profile. Required by NIIRA 2025.
Total admissible assets as a percentage of total life insurance liabilities. NAICOM requires this ratio to be maintained above 100% at all times.

The risk that proceeds from maturing short-duration instruments must be reinvested at lower interest rates than originally assumed in pricing, reducing portfolio yield relative to the liability discount rate.

The set of investment portfolios that maximise expected return for a given level of risk, or minimise risk for a given expected return. The optimal portfolio lies on the efficient frontier, subject to regulatory and ALM constraints.

Federal Government of Nigeria bond — a fixed-income instrument issued by the DMO, denominated in Naira, with maturities from 2 to 30 years. The highest-quality domestic fixed-income instrument available to Nigerian life insurers.
Nigeria’s primary fixed income and currency derivatives market, where FGN bonds, T-bills, and commercial paper are traded by institutional investors including life insurance companies.

A Board-approved document specifying the insurer’s investment objectives, risk tolerance, ALM targets, approved asset classes and limits, ALCO governance, and performance benchmarks. Mandatory under NIIRA 2025.
The risk of financial loss arising from adverse movements in exchange rates between the Naira and foreign currencies in which the insurer holds assets.
